result: Choanoflagellates are the closest living unicellular relatives to metazoans, sharing a last common ancestor (the urchoanozoan) more than 600 million years ago.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (Carr et al., 2008; King, 2004; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Steenkamp et al., 2006), representing accepted phylogenetic knowledge.

result: S. rosetta cells contain a single flagellum with a 9+2 axonemal microtubule arrangement, surrounded by 25-36 actin-based microvilli, and use planar flagellar beating for motility and feeding.
evaluation: Claims C3-C6 are supported by both current imaging data (Figure 1) and prior literature (Dayel et al., 2011; Karpov, 2016; Karpov and Leadbeater, 1998; Pettitt et al., 2002), establishing basic S. rosetta flagellar architecture.

result: Cryo-FIB milling and cryo-ET successfully visualized the S. rosetta basal apparatus, including the basal body, MTOC ring, rootlet microtubules, and flagellar vane filaments extending ~3 µm.
evaluation: Claims C7-C9 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to prior structural studies (Karpov, 2016; Pozdnyakov et al., 2017), demonstrating successful technical implementation.

result: Subtomogram averaging of >7500 axonemal repeats achieved 2.2 nm resolution, revealing that S. rosetta flagella contain outer dynein arms with two motor domains, the double-headed I1 inner dynein complex, and six single-headed inner dynein arms.
evaluation: Claims C10-C13 are well-supported by high-resolution cryo-ET data (Figure 3, Table 1) with appropriate resolution estimates (FSC criterion), providing detailed structural characterization of dynein organization.

result: S. rosetta flagella exhibit doublet-specific structural features, including replacement of ODAs and IDAs on DMT 5 by o-SUB5-6 and i-SUB5-6 structures, and a unique connection between the A-tubule and IDA c on DMT 9.
evaluation: Claims C14-C15 are supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and comparison to sea urchin structures (Lin et al., 2012b), revealing conserved and unique doublet-specific features.

result: The positional flexibility of radial spoke heads in S. rosetta was attributed to cells being frozen while flagella were actively beating.
evaluation: Claim C18 is a reasonable inference from the experimental conditions (plunge-freezing of actively swimming cells) and observed structural heterogeneity, though direct evidence of beating during freezing is not provided.

result: S. rosetta radial spoke heads resemble narrow 'ice skate' structures similar to metazoans (sea urchin, mammals) rather than the broad structures of other unicellular species (Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena), with RS1 and RS2 separated and RS2 and RS3 connected.
evaluation: Claims C19-C22 are supported by high-resolution structural data (Figures 3, 4) and extensive citations to comparative studies, establishing a key evolutionary finding about radial spoke morphology.

result: S. rosetta flagellar doublet microtubules contain many conserved MIPs (1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 2c, 3a, 3b, 6a-d), but unusually, MIP1a is shorter than MIP1b, contrary to other species.
evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by structural data (Figure 5) and comparison to prior MIP characterizations (Song et al., 2020), identifying both conserved and species-specific features.

result: A novel ~3.5 nm wide filamentous MIP (rail-MIP) was identified running along the A-tubule near protofilament A13, present in 39% of repeats with enrichment in DMTs 5-7, and its distribution may relate to proximal vs. distal flagellar location.
evaluation: Claims C25-C30 are supported by classification analyses (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1-2) showing the rail-MIP's presence, distribution, and location. The proximal/distal hypothesis (C30) is speculative but supported by observational data.

result: S. rosetta flagella contain two additional inner junction holes beyond the typical N-DRC-related hole, located near RS1 and RS3 bases, potentially representing additional PACRG subunit losses.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are supported by structural data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and citations to prior work on inner junction structure (Dymek et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Nicastro et al., 2011; Imhof et al., 2019). The PACRG loss interpretation (C34) is reasonable inference based on measured distances.

result: S. rosetta flagellar DMTs exhibit a unique ~6.5 nm gap in protofilament A2 (A2-hole), likely due to a missing tubulin dimer, present in ~39% of repeats with enrichment in DMTs 1, 5, and 6.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by classification analyses (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) showing the A2-hole's presence and distribution. The missing tubulin dimer interpretation is reasonable inference from the gap size.

result: The S. rosetta CPC has a relatively fixed orientation with the plane containing both microtubules roughly parallel to the 5-6 bridge, consistent with the flagellum's planar, sinusoidal waveform perpendicular to the CPC plane.
evaluation: Claims C37-C39 are supported by structural data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and citations to prior work on S. rosetta flagellar beating (Dayel et al., 2011; Dayel and King, 2014), establishing CPC orientation and its functional relationship to beating.

result: Subtomogram averaging of >1300 CPC repeats achieved 2.5 nm resolution, revealing that S. rosetta CPC contains all major projections with periodicities of 16 nm and 32 nm, strongly resembles sea urchin CPC (lacking C2 MIP, small C1e, prominent C1a-C2a connections), but uniquely shows partial reduction of the C1d network with apparent FAP54 loss.
evaluation: Claims C40-C46 are well-supported by high-resolution structural data (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Table 1) and extensive citations to comparative CPC studies (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019; Han et al., 2022), establishing both conserved and unique CPC features.

result: Vane filaments were clearly observed extending from the flagellar membrane on both sides of the S. rosetta flagellum, originating at the base and extending beyond tomogram/lamella widths (~1.2-3 µm), oriented parallel to the ice layer (likely due to surface tension during blotting), consistent with predicted hydrodynamic function in filter feeding.
evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are supported by extensive imaging data (Figures 2, 5—figure supplement 2A, 7) and citation to modeling work (Nielsen et al., 2017). The ice layer orientation (C50) and functional interpretation (C51) are reasonable inferences from observed orientation and prior predictions.

result: The S. rosetta flagellar vane is composed of two sheets of thin filaments extending ~80 nm from the membrane before splitting to form diamond-shaped meshes, with 1-2 rows of nodes near the membrane where filaments branch, and the two sheets separated by ~45 nm with offset nodes.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by detailed 3D structural data (Figure 7A-D) enabling unprecedented visualization of vane architecture, including measurements of filament extension, node positions, and sheet separation.

result: Vane filaments showed regional variation, with some areas highly organized and interconnected while others appeared wispy, present in 53 of 54 tomograms analyzed, and also observed within the flagellar pocket at the flagellum base.
evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by systematic analysis across multiple tomograms (Figure 7B-D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), documenting vane structural heterogeneity and distribution.

result: Previously undescribed barb-like membrane complexes (~50 nm height) were identified extending from the S. rosetta flagellar membrane, consisting of a top knob, central rod with wider mid-body, and four arms connecting to the membrane. Subtomogram averaging of 600 particles with fourfold symmetry achieved 2.5 nm resolution. Barb numbers varied (0-22 per tomogram) but were consistently located near vane filament bases (median 50 nm distance). The central rod lumen is not continuous and the base appears weakly membrane-connected. Barbs were also observed in the flagellar pocket but not on co-cultured E. pacifica bacteria.
evaluation: Claims C60-C68 are well-supported by high-resolution structural data (Figure 7E-K, Table 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) including subtomogram averaging, quantitative distance measurements, and systematic survey across tomograms and bacterial controls, establishing a novel flagellar structure.

result: The structure and organization of dyneins, radial spokes, and CPC in S. rosetta are consistent with metazoan flagella, suggesting these features were present in the urchoanozoan ancestor, pre-dating the transition to multicellularity.
evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by comprehensive structural comparisons throughout the manuscript (Figures 3-6) showing S. rosetta's similarity to metazoans rather than other unicellular species. The evolutionary inference (C70) is reasonable based on phylogenetic position and observed structural similarities.

result: Most unicellular species contain three outer dynein heads per ODA while multicellular species typically contain two (consistent with genomic data showing loss in metazoans and excavates). Similarly, unicellular organisms have broad RS head structures with connections between all three heads, whereas metazoans have narrow RS heads with RS1 and RS2 separated. Metazoan CPC orientation is fixed with stable C1a-C2a connections and reduced C1e projection.
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by comparative structural data (Figure 4) and extensive citations to prior structural and genomic studies (Lin et al., 2014; Nicastro et al., 2006; Pigino et al., 2012; Kollmar, 2016; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021; Carbajal-González et al., 2013), establishing key unicellular vs. multicellular differences.

result: Loss of bulkier flagellar structures (third dynein head, broad RS heads, larger CPC projections) may have generated space for additional molecular components in the choanoflagellate-animal ancestor. Animal cilia/flagella have adapted many additional signaling functions compared to unicellular eukaryotes. The reduced structures in S. rosetta could relate to a shift from predator avoidance to increased signaling in more stable environments, or loss of selection pressure for the third dynein head in single-flagellum organisms.
evaluation: Claims C76-C80 are explicitly speculative ("we can speculate," "could be related") evolutionary hypotheses. While supported by citation to animal ciliary signaling functions (Bloodgood, 2010; Mitchell, 2007; Sigg et al., 2017), these remain untested hypotheses requiring additional comparative data and functional studies.

result: The combination of rail-MIP and A2-hole may provide strength and flexibility to compensate for loss of bulkier flagellar structures in S. rosetta. The rail-MIP may provide mechanical support to compensate for external forces such as drag from the flagellar vane.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are speculative functional interpretations based on known MIP functions (Owa et al., 2019) and structural observations. While the rail-MIP discovery is well-supported, its proposed compensatory function and mechanical role require experimental validation through functional studies or computational modeling.

result: The choanoflagellate flagellar vane has been observed in only a few of >125 known species, previously described as a bilateral fringe of delicate perpendicular glycocalyx fibers extending approximately two-thirds of flagellar length. The wispy hairs observed in S. rosetta appear similar to 'partially disintegrated' vanes in Monosiga sp., suggesting they may represent a common structural variation rather than disintegration.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by citations to prior vane observations (Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014) and comparison with current data. The reinterpretation of wispy structures (C85) is reasonable inference from improved preservation.

result: The choanoflagellate vane differs significantly from other flagellar appendages (mastigonemes, tripartite hairs). Algal mastigonemes are ~10 nm diameter with two intertwined filaments, while choanoflagellate vane filaments are ~3.5 nm arranged as wispy hairs or meshes. No connections were detected between vane filament membrane anchors and axonemal microtubules, and BLAST searches found no homologues of mastigoneme proteins MST1 and PKD2 in the S. rosetta genome.
evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by structural comparisons (current data vs. Liu et al., 2020; Bouck, 1971; Hibberd, 1975) and BLAST analysis results, establishing that the vane is structurally and molecularly distinct from other flagellar appendages.

result: The choanoflagellate vane morphology was proposed to be similar to sponge choanocyte flagellar vanes (bilateral, wing-like, membrane-anchored without axonemal connections). However, sponge choanocyte vanes appear narrower, denser, more massive, and often connect to collar microvilli. The choanoflagellate vane was previously reported to span the collar width in Monosiga brevicolis, but the current tomogram field of view did not capture vane ends to assess microvilli connections.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by citations to prior comparative studies (Mehl and Reiswig, 1991; Brunet and King, 2017; Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014), acknowledging both similarities and differences between choanoflagellate and sponge vanes, with appropriate acknowledgment of current data limitations.

result: Fibers originating within the flagellar pocket suggest the vane could be secreted from the cell membrane before flagellar transport. Large fiber-filled vesicles have been observed near the apical part of choanoflagellate cells following division (when flagellum/vane would regenerate). Glycosyltransferases (jumble, couscous) localize to the basal pole and flagellar/collar base, and the collar base stains positively for lectins indicating carbohydrate chains near the flagellum. Proteinase K digest failed to remove the vane, supporting a carbohydrate or glycoprotein-based rather than proteinaceous composition.
evaluation: Claims C94-C98 are supported by observational data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), citations to prior localization studies (Leadbeater, 2014; Wetzel et al., 2018), and experimental proteinase K digest results. The vane secretion hypothesis (C94) is reasonable inference, and the carbohydrate composition conclusion (C98) is supported by the proteinase K resistance, though the authors appropriately note additional characterization is needed.

result: The barbs' location alongside the vane suggests they could play a role in vane generation or maintenance. The barb top knobs resemble the size and shape of vane nodes. The S. rosetta genome has undergone extensive horizontal gene transfer from bacteria, so barbs could have ancient bacterial origin. Barb structures most closely resemble an uncharacterized bacterial complex in Prosthecobacter debontii (though with fourfold vs. fivefold symmetry).
evaluation: Claims C99-C102 are speculative functional and evolutionary hypotheses. While the structural observations (C100) and genomic context (C101, supported by Matriano et al., 2021) are valid, and the bacterial complex comparison (C102, Dobro et al., 2017) is interesting, the proposed vane-related function (C99) and bacterial origin remain untested hypotheses requiring additional evidence.

result: Choanoflagellate flagella more closely resemble human flagella than other protist model systems (Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena), and may represent an attractive alternative model system for studying human ciliopathies.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by the comprehensive structural comparisons throughout the manuscript showing S. rosetta's similarity to metazoan (including human) flagella in dynein number, RS morphology, and CPC structure. The proposed utility for ciliopathy research (C104) is reasonable inference from these similarities, though explicitly speculative ("may represent").

result: S. rosetta was co-cultured with E. pacifica as a food source. Cryo-FIB milling was performed using a 30 keV gallium ion beam with 30 pA for initial milling/thinning and 10 pA for final polishing, producing ~150 nm lamellae. Tilt series images were collected using a K3 Summit detector at ×26,000 magnification under low-dose conditions in counting mode. The cumulative electron dose per tilt series was limited to 100 e-/Å².
evaluation: Claims C105-C108 are methodological details supported by the Materials and Methods section and citation to culture protocols (Levin and King, 2013). These are standard, well-documented procedures appropriate for cryo-ET studies.
